translations.text: Whenever those honored before us received the grace of God and sounded their devout melodies, we too were all there with you.
United in the word of truth, we learned the same things, rejoiced in the same things, and took delight in them.
None of those who understand what is good [?] takes any joy for himself, but directs everything toward the glory of God.
Whoever agrees with the speaker shares with the giver, for by praising the speaker he worships the one who is proclaimed.

Our fathers taught us this conduct, free from envy, especially our father, who is the head of all the fathers, sits on the honorable throne above them all, and has a mind clear and free from jealousy.
He himself first composes the skillful spiritual utterance and makes it sound melodiously in everyone's ears: “Who would grant that all the people of God were prophets?”
Such a spirit glorifies its Lord and regards the words and good qualities of others as its own.
If anyone corrupts the words of others, he turns not against the one who received the gifts, but against the one who gave them.
Thoughts are revealed in faces. Look at the father of us all: with what a cheerful face and kindly eyes he looks at us who speak and at you who listen!
Whenever you see someone's face cast downward, recognize the deceit in his thoughts.
Whenever his face hangs downward, know that his heart is devising deceit. As the Scriptures also say, “Whoever winks with his eye devises deceit.”
Christ is glorified, and the world is enlightened; but the one who has evil in his mind sits deeply wounded, stricken in his heart and torn in his liver.
And because we have encountered a father who is holy and free from envy, we learned without deceit and will give without envy.
Let us begin the sequence that we were following yesterday and left unfinished because of the abundance of various thoughts pouring in from here and there.
Our intention was to explain a little of the beginning of the Gospel. But we do not know how the dispute with the heretics that arose in our midst drove us away from there.

We are not passing from one exposition of the word to another, but attending to the same subject and the same thoughts. Christ is glorified, and the battle against those who fight against Christ is set in order.
Let every disease be cast out! Let those who today celebrate the scandalous and delusive feast be ashamed—a name alone, devoid of the truth of what is right.
Those who have put on Christ celebrate Passover with the Jews. Those clothed in Christ share fellowship with those who fight against Christ.
I call them clothed in Christ because of the name they profess. But what fellowship can light have with darkness?
Or what agreement can the Jews have with Christ? Or what likeness is there between the table of Christ and the Jews' [?] table?
The children of devotion to God celebrate Passover with dogs. Those who ought to sing praises with the angels howl with dogs.
The devout person praises God with the angels: “I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart; before your angels I will sing psalms to you.”
The devout person glorifies God with the angels, but whoever destroys the order of the Church celebrates the feast with dogs.
And because these are words not of insult but of truth and rebuke, listen to Paul, the great preacher, who says, “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers.”
Those who have received the heavenly lamps hold the lighting of lamps with the Jews. Those who have received the Lamb of God and celebrate Passover slaughter sheep with the Jews.
Oh, the foolishness! The shadow seeks to destroy the truth, and those who have received the truth follow shadows.
They follow shadows. Why do you light a lamp among the Jews? Is it not so that your name [?] may be extinguished from the Gospel?
Whoever gives hospitality to a rebel and lends the rebel support will suffer the same punishment along with him.
Listen to David: “If you saw thieves, you went along with them, and you cast your lot with adulterers.” If only it were with adulterers, and not with [?]!

Adultery and sexual immorality, although their names and deeds are filthy and disgusting and deserve the punishment of eternal torment, are nevertheless sins committed by human beings against human beings, and by servants against fellow servants.
But sinning against God surpasses every other sin, just as offenses that someone commits against [?] are more serious than those committed against a fellow servant.
Likewise, when someone fights against God, those sins are more grievous than all other sins. Why do you, a child of godliness, become [?] with the children of destruction?
If you saw someone under a king’s punishment and in [?] before the royal presence, would you want to enter into friendship with him?
Would you not, even if you already had a friendship with him, break that off too, so that you might escape punishment?
Let us see where the Jews stand and what condition the Christians are in.

Listen to the holy Gospel: “Whoever believes in the Son,” it says, “receives eternal life; and whoever disobeys the Son will not see life.” The living celebrate a festival with those who are not alive.
What good thing have the Jews devised? What order of worship have they preserved uncorrupted, that you should add from them some necessary support to the Church’s beautiful practices?
Do you not hear the prophet who says, “You, house of Israel, have corrupted all your young people and falsified the truth”?
For they renounced godliness and sold it, because they paid no heed.
Indeed, they did not even keep their wine pure. Is this not the very first accusation against them from the prophet Isaiah? “Your merchants,” he says, “mix water with wine.”
If only the heretics today also mixed water with wine, and not God with created beings!
See the prophets’ accusation against the Jews in writing—an accusation that the apostles also proclaim openly. Listen to the great preacher Paul, who writes to the Thessalonians:
“I do not want you to be unaware, brothers,” he says, “that you too suffered the same afflictions from your own countrymen as the Church of God did from the Jews—
from the Jews who killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets and persecuted us, who displeased God and opposed humanity.”
Do you become a partner of those who are under immeasurable punishments? To such people Isaiah says, “That is your portion, and that same lot is your inheritance.”
I would like to learn from them why they celebrate the festival at all, and for what hope.
Since they remove repentance from their midst, whom do they worship? [?] the vain and the acceptable, and the worship of the foolish.
They deprive of hope for repentance those who need repentance more than anyone. Burning with mange, they also reject the physician.
They parade the name Cathari, which means “holy ones,” yet they have holiness neither in body nor in mind.
Nothing so angers God, provokes him to wrath, and makes someone liable to the punishment of great torments as when someone calls himself holy.
Even if he is free from every sin, he must count himself among sinners.
Listen to Saint John: “Little children, if we sin, we are not of God”; and again: “Whoever does evil is not of God.”

When he gave the exhortation not to sin, he then brought forward the truth. The same man who said, “Whoever sins is not of God,” humbling himself still further, says: “If we say that we have not sinned, we lie.”
He gave an exhortation to vigilance, and did not deny the power. He looked to the teaching of the truth, and also saw how readily the mind stumbles.
But now the enemies of reverence for God hold feasts and demand proof of deeds, yet they have departed from every firm foundation.
I too wished to raise such matters with you who love Christ, and to show that this opposition is futile, an empty opinion.
When someone departs from the order of the church, he does not remain [?]; rather, error seizes him and carries him away, as when torrents of rivers flow into the sea.
What do Easter and the feast make known? What is accomplished on the day of the feast? Are not Christ’s sufferings and resurrection proclaimed?
Salvation is announced to the world, and every soul is enlightened by the divine word.
And now, how can this be? Do we have this seal and pledge of worship only on one day in the year? Is not every Sunday the church’s Easter?
Is the sacrifice on that day different from the sacrifice on this day? Is the enjoyment of the mysteries at Easter different from that on Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday?
Whenever you commemorate Christ’s sufferings, you celebrate Easter.
Formerly, lambs were sacrificed once a year, but Christ’s sacrifice is offered continually.
Therefore the giver of life, making it clear that the mystery is not subject to times and days, or months and years, says to the disciples:
“As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you shall proclaim my death.”
Who, then, celebrates that feast? Whoever celebrates the same mystery celebrates Easter continually.
“And if the mystery is celebrated continually,” they say, “what need is there for a new feast?”
A great deal. Such things have often been given by God to console our human nature and weakness:
God’s mystery always stands immovable and firm, as do the altar, the priests, the sacrifices, the services, and everything performed in his name.
But because God saw human weakness, entangled with earthly affairs and defiled by various impurities, he established a remedy for it through the holy apostles: the feast of Easter,
so that those who at all times are entangled in sins, fixed upon earthly concerns, and unwilling to look toward the light of worship
might at least be drawn to look by the name of the feast, and through remembrance of the life-giving sufferings prepare themselves to partake of the holy things.

Feasts are for gathering many people in one place, but for the saints there are feasts continually. What are the saints’ feasts? Blessing God. Therefore whoever blesses him continually celebrates [?] feasts.
And listen to David, who says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will continually be in my mouth.” Whoever blesses [?] always celebrates a feast.
The names of Easter, of [?], and of the feasts at which everyone gathers signify the gathering of many people in one place, to enlighten those in darkness and to bring back those who have strayed,
for correcting stubborn ways, for raising the dead and buried, and for being in every respect an edification of all the members of Christ.
But it is no wonder that those who broke away from the church should also separate themselves from the feast. For if they had been of us, they would have remained with us.
But let the corrupting feast be condemned by the faithful, and let our feast shine brightly at its proper time—not as though grace were subject to times.
For every order and arrangement is to be established in the church. Let us now turn to the course of the discourse.
Let us speak and preach, not regarding the preaching as something of our own, but rendering service to our holy father. Let us pay the overdue debt owed to our father's words.
I say this so that no one, being unaware of these matters, may accuse us of appropriating for ourselves the time allotted to our father's teaching.
For we do what we are commanded, and we necessarily follow our father's wishes.
Yesterday, brothers, our task was to proclaim and explain briefly the teaching about God at the beginning of the Gospel, and to show what intention the words make clear.
John says, “In the beginning was the Word.” He did not say, “In the beginning was the Son,” or “the Only-begotten.”
He strengthened the minds of his hearers, lest, because of their minds' weakness in understanding the teaching about God, the divine birth should be distorted by human notions.
For among us, whenever birth is discussed, notions of a father and mother enter in, along with the solidity of the body and the causes of passions.
He first conceals the name “Son” and introduces the designation “Word,” so that by the designation “Word” he may explain the freedom from passion of both the begetter and the birth.
And, to repeat this once more, he calls him “Word” to show that the birth is not subject to passions.
“And he was with God,” he says, to make clear that his honor is undivided.
He said that he was with God and made it known that he is God. Then he also introduces creation: “Everything came into being through him.”
Let the futile labor of those who dispute be exposed: through the expressions “through him” and “by him,” they wish to establish an inferiority in the honor of the Only-begotten.
But perhaps someone will say, “Write that the heretics demanded an explanation and cannot say what ‘through him’ means and what ‘by him’ means.
You, who belong to the church, explain what ‘through him’ means and what ‘by him’ means.”
The divine Scriptures do not employ technical language or submit to the constructions of human thought.
For they are not Aristotelian teachings or Platonic distinctions, but simple faith, without deceit or cunning, and full of great freedom.
When he says “through him” and “by him,” he means “from him.” “Everything through him”—what does “through him” mean? Precisely this: “from him.”
When he says, “Let the waters bring forth,” and “Let the earth produce,” does he call the water and the earth creators?

Or when Paul says, “The first man was from the earth, made of dust,” is the earth the creator? And when he says, “Man did not come from woman, but woman from man,” does that make the man the woman's creator?
Do you see that [?] “from him” does not always apply to the creator, but also to some material involved?

And it is clear that saying “by him” and “through him” of the giver of life does not present him as some material put to use. Rather, he established in existence what did not exist and called what was not into being.
God's will is not like the material and timber used by craftsmen, nor is it God's essence.

For his works do not come out of God's essence; rather, his will brings what is not into being and what does not exist into existence. He wills, and everything comes to be; he gives a sign, and everything obeys.
Now, when he says “from him,” this stands for saying “from the Father's will”; and when he says “through him” and “by him,” this means “from the Son's power.”
And to dismiss these excuses made by those who offer excuses for sins, the blessed Paul says:
“Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has lent him anything and will receive repayment? For everything is from him and through him.”
If “through him” indicates some inferiority, and “from him” a superiority in honor, how can he speak here of both with reference to the same person?

Would he mix things that cannot be mixed? And if “from him” indicates a superiority in honor, how can he speak here of both with reference to the same person? Would he mix things that cannot be mixed?
Of whom do they suppose it was said, “Everything is from him and through him”—the Father or the Son?
If it was said of the Father, then see: they have brought the Father down to “by him” and “through him,” if “by him” means service.
And if they have declared that “through him” means this, it would be a great insult to say of the Father “from him,” “by him,” and “through him,” for one person cannot be both master and servant.
But was it said of the Son? Look: it does not say only “through him” and “by him,” but also “from him.” And one person cannot be both a servant and one who acts on his own authority.
Rather, to clear away our delusions, he brought both expressions together with reference to one person,
so that you may learn that words do not divide God's nature. Rather, “from him,” “by him,” “through him,” and “in him” were said of the same person—sometimes of the Father and sometimes of the Son.

And since they frequently repeat “by whom” and “through him,” and thereby suppose that the Son has a position of service, inferiority, and lesser rank, it is necessary to gather the prophetic words and set them before you.

While the blessed Joseph was in prison—he who overcame every evil through humility—he saw there the eunuchs of Pharaoh the king with sorrowful faces, their expressions revealing the grief of their hearts.
“Why,” he says, “do you have sorrowful faces today?” “We have had a dream,” they say, “and there is no one to interpret it for us.”
And what did the blessed Joseph say to this? “Tell me the dream,” he says. And he did not say that its interpretation is “from God,” but “through God.”
If that is so, are you exalted, while God becomes a servant? Is not the interpretation indeed “through him”?
You ought to have said that it is “from God.” Do you speak through God and by God, or does God speak through you and by you?
Now, do not submit to the weakness of words. Listen to God's gifts and to the Old Testament.
“These are the ordinances and commandments that Moses, the servant of the Lord, commanded at the Lord's command”—if the commands are through Moses.
Pay attention: “These,” he says, “are the ordinances and commandments that Moses commanded.” And he did not say “God through Moses,” but “Moses through God.”
He said “Word,” called him “God,” and named him “Creator.” And little by little he proceeds gently to the designation “only-begotten Son.”

“Everything,” he says, “came into being through him.” He proclaims his work of creation. “And without him nothing came into being” among the things that came into being, not among those of the uncreated nature.
Do you remember the first words we spoke—that the Scriptures speak with reference to the matters before them, indicating something?
For the disciples of the heretics, who wage war against the Holy Spirit, also take “Everything came into being through him” as a blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.
Everything came into being through him—everything that came into being, and [?] the uncreated nature.

When the giver of life says, “All who came before me were thieves and robbers,” will you accuse Moses of being a thief, and Isaiah of being a robber? Does he not call those to whom these words referred thieves and robbers?
Everything came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being that came into being. In him was life.
He said that he is the Word, and called him God; he said that he was with God, and named him Creator. He also calls him Life, because the Creator is certainly also the giver of life.
It is impossible for him to be the Creator and not give his creatures the power to live. He was Life, because he possesses the gifts that give life and light.

For whatever I have established needs life and the light of living existence, and cannot enjoy light without life. For this reason he adds in the same passage that he was Life, and that the life was the light of humanity.
He showed the creative power that gives life and light. Then he says, “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.”

Where the discourse concerns God, it says, “He was,” and where it concerns a man, “He came into being.” “He came as a witness, to testify about the light, so that all might be strengthened through him.”
The heretic finds [?]. “Do you see,” he says, “that ‘through him’ indicates service? For it is through the prophets themselves that God becomes credible.”
But notice: although human nature is subject to laws and to the Lord’s service, here “through whom”—
does not indicate any service, but the declaration and proclamation of the prophets. For he became a witness to the light willingly, not unwillingly.
But if they remain exceedingly contentious and arrogant, and regard “through whom” and “through him” as indications of service, let them hear Paul, who says:
“God is faithful, through whom you were called into obedience to his Son.” Here, moreover, “through whom” and “through him” do not lead from the Son to the Father, but from the Father to the Son.

“He was here in the world,” he says, and, “He came into the world.” And because he said that he came into the world, lest anyone suppose that the incorporeal one changed his location, he says, “He was in this world, and he came into the world.”
How, then, do they say, “Whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world”? Being sent does not indicate any change of place, but the manifestation of the saving dispensation.
And listen to how this can be: Where does wheat appear from? Where does wine come from? Where does oil come from? Is it not from the earth?
Why, then, did God say, “See, I am sending you wheat, wine, and oil”?
If the wheat that is sent does not come from heaven, but its being sent is shown by the appearance of the plant,
do you suppose that the incorporeal Creator—Being from true Being, and Existence from true Existence—is sent by a change of place, rather than by the manifestation of the saving dispensation?
For if the Son was sent from place to place, then the Father remained only there above, and the Son came only here below. The Son would not be in heaven, nor the Father on earth.
Pay close attention. If you cling slavishly to the wording and understand the sending of the Son as though he were somehow separated from the one who sent him,
it will necessarily follow that the one sent from heaven is only on earth and is separated from heaven, while the sender is not on earth but is confined to heaven.
And who would be so impious and lawless, sharpening a tongue that fights against God, as to confine the Father to heaven alone and enclose the Son only on earth?
Do you wish to learn some true teaching about God, not spoken idly but attested by the Scriptures?
The Son was sent, yet remained on high; he ascended into heaven, yet is with us. These are not words of my own, but those of the Life-giver himself.

“The one whom the Father sanctified and sent,” he says. It seems, in a way, that he departed from the one who sent him. Yet how does the one who was sent say, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”?
And again: “The Father who sent me is with me.” If he is with you, then you were not sent alone, but were sent with him.

If you understand him to have been sent in the bodily sense of sending, how can he say of the Father who sent him, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” and again, “The one who sent me is with me”?
So that someone hearing “The one who sent me is with me” should not suppose this to mean some active power rather than the Father himself, he makes the statement clear elsewhere:
“The Father who dwells in me,” he says, “does the works.” It is the one who dwells in me, not the one who produces effects in me.
He came from heaven and remained there in heaven; he ascended from earth and did not depart from earth. And to show that these are not my words, listen to the Lord himself:
“I ascend,” he says, “to the Father, and I will send the Holy Spirit to you.” “I ascend” indicates separation, and “I will send” indicates the absence of separation.
So that no one should consider his bodily ascent a change in his divinity, he commands the disciples:
“Go, make disciples of all nations, and baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. And behold, I am with you every day until the end of the world.”
What does “I am with you” mean? We recognize the meaning from the very expression: he who spoke in the prophets then now performs mighty deeds.
“Go and make disciples of all nations, and behold, I am with you.” Who said this? Clearly, it was the one who spoke through the prophet Haggai:
“Now be strong, Zerubbabel,” says the Lord, “and let the hands of my people be strengthened, and work in my house, for I am with you, and my Spirit remains among you.”
God is everywhere and with all believers: the Father is among believers, the Son is among believers, and the Holy Spirit is among believers.
And as for how the Father is among believers, listen to the prophet who says: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion; rejoice and exult with all your heart,
for the Lord has removed your afflictions from you and rescued you from the hands of your enemies. He will reign in your midst; the Lord will reign in your midst, and you will no longer see evils.”
Behold, the Father has been shown reigning among believers. And what of the Son? “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I too am among them.”
The Father is among them, the Son is among them, and the Holy Spirit is among them: “For I am with you,” says the Lord Almighty, “and the Spirit remains among you.”
Why do you divide what is indivisible? [?] You break apart what cannot be broken apart. For I am speaking of the body that he united to himself, and no one dares say that it is separate.
I know that I have spoken about this before in this discourse, but we should not look back at what was said earlier and leave aside the teaching when the occasion calls for it.
For the purpose of these words is not to avoid going over the same things, but to avoid departing from them.
The disciples of the heretics say, “See how the Son shares equal honor with us.
‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.’ See how the Son calls the Father his God.”

And now, before everything else, we must consider that the only-begotten Word, the impassible being, the incorruptible and unchangeable power, came to his own creation and united the flesh to himself.
He did not himself descend into lowliness, but raised its lowliness to greatness.
And see how he makes a heavenly exchange with humanity. For anyone who makes an exchange gives and receives: he took flesh from us and gave us the Spirit from himself.
Just as you, whose God and Lord he is, would not dare to call God Father if you had not received the Spirit from him, so the Son would not call the Father his God if he had not taken flesh from you.
For the Life-giver knew that his Father and our Father are not Father in the same way, and that his God and our God are not God in the same manner, so he distinguishes the names:
“To my Father and to your Father,” for he is mine in one way and yours in another; “and to my God and to your God,” for he is your God in one way and mine in another.
Because of the flesh taken from you, my Father became my God; and because of the Spirit received from me, he became the God and Father of the world.
You could not call the Father the God of me, the Son, if I had not taken flesh; nor would you have any means of calling God Father if you had not received the Spirit.
And Paul bears witness: “Because you are sons,” he says, “God sent the Spirit of his Son, who cries out in your hearts, ‘Abba, Father.’”
“I ascend to my Father by nature and to your Father by grace; to your God by nature and to my God according to my flesh.”
John says, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.”
“Why,” they say, “did he not mention the Spirit? [?] the Son of God was revealed, and he kept silent about the Spirit?”
We must understand this, brothers: the teachings of the mysteries are one thing, and public proclamation is another.

The apostles preached religious teachings in their proclamation, but handed down the truth in the mysteries. For it was not possible to trust unresponsive ears and openly present teachings about the Trinity.
Pay attention to what Christ says to the apostles: “I still have many things to say to you, which you cannot bear now.”
The apostles, who were born among the Jews as worshipers of God, into a faith that worshiped God, who walked with Christ and saw the signs with their own eyes,
and beheld God the Word in the flesh, could not bear to hear everything at once. But how could those from among the Gentiles, who had only just escaped from temples and blood,
and idols and many gods—and some had not yet even escaped—immediately be shown the account of the divine dispensation?
The opponent of the Spirit says, “Everywhere in the Scriptures I find the Father and the Son mentioned, but silence about the Spirit.
“First, the Life-giver himself says that no one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father. Did he perhaps say, ‘the Holy Spirit’?
“‘No one knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son.’ And he did not include the Spirit with the Father and the Son.
“Now how can one who [?] is not capable of knowing the Father be counted as belonging to that same Godhead?”
If the Son’s knowing here has sharpened your tongue to blaspheme the Spirit, what will you do if elsewhere you see it said that the Spirit knows the Father, without mentioning the Son?
“No one has ascended into heaven,” and “No one knows the Father except the Son”: this is the utterance of the Life-giver. And the same utterance speaks in Paul.
For he indeed says, “If you wish to obtain proof of Christ, who speaks to you through me.” And what will the voice of Christ say through Paul?
No one knows the things of a person except that person's spirit. Likewise, no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.
If you reject the Spirit there, then here too you will separate the Son [?]. But if the Son is without division here, then the Spirit is also without separation there.
There is also another way: sometimes he mentions only the Father and says nothing about the Son or the Spirit.
And sometimes he mentions only the Son and says nothing about the Father or the Spirit; and sometimes only the Spirit, and says nothing about the Father or the Son.

Again, very often he mentions two together: the Father and the Son, while saying nothing about the Spirit; or the Son and the Spirit, while saying nothing about the Father. Where he mentions the Father, will he say nothing about the Son?
Once the apostles asked Christ, "Lord, teach us to pray."
He taught them the prayer and said, "Pray like this: Our Father in heaven, may your name be holy," and the rest, one phrase after another, to the end of the prayer.
And there he makes no mention either of himself or of the Spirit. Here is mention of the Father alone, with silence about the glory of the Son and the Spirit.
He is not denying anything, but for a beneficial and mysterious purpose he remains silent for a time about the Spirit and the Son.
"Our Father, who are in heaven." Here only the Father is mentioned. And elsewhere, see what the Giver of life himself, who taught the disciples to pray to the Father alone, says:
"Whatever you ask of me, I will do for you." And he makes no mention of the Father—not to deny the Father in any way, but to speak of his equally honored majesty.
And elsewhere he mentions only the Spirit and says nothing about the Father or the Son: "John baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit."
In the Holy Spirit alone? And what does the explicit instruction concerning the mystery declare? "Baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."

Again, he speaks of the Father and the Son and says nothing about the Spirit. "There is one God, the Father," he says, "from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things."
For Paul's words at that time were not about matters of religion, but about doing away with the many gods.
Study, and you will find the solution. As the Giver of life also says, "Search the Scriptures," not thoughts.
Do not put your trust in the delusions of thoughts, but listen to Scripture. "The thoughts of mortals," he says, "are fearful, and their minds are wavering."

And again the Savior says, "That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you sent," and he says nothing about the Spirit. Elsewhere he mentions the Father and the Spirit and says nothing about the Son,
according to the testimony cited above: "Enter and work in my house," says the Lord Almighty, "for I am with you, and my Spirit remains among you."
And where would the Son be? For he says, "I and my Spirit." And elsewhere Paul mentions the Son and the Spirit and says nothing about the Father:
"Neither adulterers," he says, "nor the sexually immoral, nor thieves, nor drunkards, nor slanderers will inherit the kingdom of God. And some of you were such people."

"But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God." And where would the Father be? "Search the Scriptures," he says, and do not search thoughts.
Let us also state some clear facts that reveal the lawlessness of the heretics. The apostle says, "The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit, for they seem foolish to him."
The Gentile does not stumble, because he considers the preaching foolishness; the Jew stumbles over Christ. And what does Paul say about this?
“We,” he says, “preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles.” Why does the Gentile consider the preaching foolishness?
Tell him that God made Christ as one of the creatures, and he does not argue, but says, “The Creator was able to do that.”
Say that he was begotten, and he mocks and considers the statement foolishness. “Can God be begotten,” he says, “whose nature has no needs?”
Consider what sort of people the heretics share their lot with. The Gentiles disparage the accounts of the begetting as foolishness.
And you divide and alter the begetting, and introduce a creature in place of the begetting. You are found stumbling with the Jews and considering the preaching foolishness with the Gentiles.
We, brothers, are not heretics. We do not approach the mystery impatiently, but are enlightened by faith.
You see God proclaimed in the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Before the mystery, the prophets glorified the mystery. And do you alter the mystery proclaimed in prophecy?
God spoke through the prophets as from one person, and at the same time imparted knowledge of the Son and the Spirit.
And since the apostles did not later preach just one, to show the certainty of these things God says something like this through the prophet Joel:
“It shall be in the last days,” says God. Pay attention, for steadfast souls and attentive minds are needed here, so as not to forget the divine proclamation.
“And it shall be in the last days,” says God, “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh.” For the moment he has spoken only of himself and the Spirit, but he will also explain about the Son.
And what will he do? For this is not a time of proclamation or of openly revealed religion, but of hidden mysteries.
He brings forward a certain intermediate person, interwoven like a parable [?], and, many words later, at the end he imparts knowledge of the Son.
Lest, by making the knowledge explicit, occasions for sin arise for those who cannot understand the circumstances of these things, for the moment he mentions himself and the Spirit:
“I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams.”
And see how, while he is still speaking of himself and the Spirit, he gently imparts knowledge of the Son as well:

“And I will give signs in heaven above and on earth below: blood and fire and billowing smoke. The sun shall turn to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes.”

And will that day not be yours, but another Lord’s? For you announce good news as though about another Lord. If you who are speaking are God, and you will pour out of your own Spirit, how do you announce good news about another Lord?
It is indeed clear that he calls the Son, who is from himself, Lord: “Before the day of the Lord comes, which is great and glorious.”
For the first coming took place in meekness and calm. He is not speaking of that one, but of the great and glorious coming, whose glory is manifest.
And what follows this? “And it shall be,” he says, “that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” He did not say, “Whoever calls upon my name shall be saved.”
And lest the victory of the truth seem forced, I will bring Paul forward as a witness. What name shall we call upon and be saved?
Paul, the tongue of truth and interpreter of the sayings of the prophets, says, “Is he the God of the Jews only, and not of the Gentiles?
Yes, of the Gentiles also, since God is one, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith.”
And elsewhere: God himself exalts all who call upon him, and everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.
And to make it clear that he applies the saying to Christ, the prophecy says: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.
And the apostle explains: How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him in whom they have not believed?
And how shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without someone preaching? And how shall they preach unless they are sent?

As it is also written: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace, who bring good news of good things! He revealed himself, he also revealed the Holy Spirit, and he also revealed the Son.
And just as at the beginning of the prophecy he spoke beforehand of himself and of the Spirit, so at its conclusion he seals the meaning of the prophecy with the Son.

For from Mount Zion, he says, shall come the one who is saved, and those who have received the good news, whom the Lord called to himself. By those who have received the good news, he means the messengers of the good news, who were called by the Lord.
Jesus, he says, called the twelve apostles and gave them authority over demons and unclean spirits.
And elsewhere, to show the royal and divine splendor of the Holy Spirit, the Spirit says concerning Paul and Barnabas:
Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for a work to which I am going to call them. And this much up to this point.
May the believers be enlightened, and may the opponents feel shame and turn back. There is no need for toil: stand in awe of the word; receive salvation.
God once threatened the people of Jerusalem through the prophet, saying: Behold, I will destroy them and reduce them to nothing.
And when the Lord saw that their hearts had repented, the Lord said to the man of God: Do you see how they felt shame? I will not destroy them.
Through the prayers of the holy fathers, may they too turn back, may we be strengthened, and may the church be glorified in Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
